The Board · Special Report

One phone, five continents, and a single company that owns none of the factories

An iPhone begins as brine, rock and quartz sand, and ends as the most profitable object in consumer electronics. This is the whole journey, and at every stop, the same two questions: how is it physically done, and who gets paid.

By Josh Pilcher
Scroll

The Atacama, Chile

Every phone starts as a hole in the ground.

Brine, rock and quartz sand go in one end. The most profitable object in consumer electronics comes out the other.

Photograph via Council on Foreign Relations. Evaporation ponds in the Atacama, where lithium brine spends a year or more concentrating before it becomes battery chemical.

Verdict

Apple does not manufacture the iPhone. It designs the phone in California and Austin, then buys almost every physical act from someone else.

The brain is made in Taiwan. TSMC is the only company that can fabricate it at Apple’s scale.

The screen comes mainly from South Korea. The camera sensors come from Japan. Most materials become usable chemicals or metals in China.

Hands in China and India do the final assembly. It is the most photographed step, and the least valuable one.

The money follows scarcity. Apple keeps about 37 cents of gross profit from each hardware dollar, while TSMC keeps close to 60 cents.

Foxconn keeps about 6 cents gross and 2 cents net. Apple has spent twenty years making sure another assembler can take its place.

Governments learned the same lesson. China subsidized an assembly city, India pays more than the assembler earns, and a tariff gap recently moved production faster than speeches did.

The phone is a stack of chokepoints above an assembly hall. The hall can move, and it has. The chokepoints have barely moved at all.

Chapter One

The Dirt

Before it is a product, it is a hole in the ground on four continents, and a chemistry lesson nobody in the West bothered to learn.

Every iPhone begins somewhere else. It begins as brine under a salt flat, rock in a pit, and quartz in the ground.

In Chile’s Atacama, lithium brine is pumped into turquoise ponds. Sun and air concentrate it for a year or more.

Other rock comes from terraced mines in Chile and Western Australia. Each pit supplies a different ingredient in the finished phone.

Two mines near Spruce Pine, North Carolina, supply an estimated 70 to 90% of the world’s high-purity quartz.

That quartz matters because chip crystals grow inside crucibles made from it. The vessel is part of the supply chain too.

An iPhone is geology made dense. It contains lithium, cobalt, copper, gold, tin, tungsten, rare earths, aluminum, and sand.

Almost none of the original rock survives recognition. Refining removes nearly everything that made it rock. Silicon shows the standard. Quartz is cooked with carbon in an electric arc furnace at about 1,800 to 2,000 degrees Celsius.

The furnace strips away oxygen. What remains is metallurgical silicon, about 98 to 99.5% pure. That purity serves most industries. Chipmakers treat it as a starting material, not a product.

The silicon is converted into trichlorosilane. As a liquid, it can be distilled repeatedly until unwanted elements are separated out.

It is then deposited onto heated rods in the Siemens process. The rods grow into polysilicon with nine to eleven nines of purity.

At that level, impurities fall below one part per billion. The number sounds excessive until the chip’s own arithmetic enters.

A processor works by adding dopant atoms on purpose. Their concentrations range from a hundred trillion to a hundred quintillion per cubic centimetre.

One phosphorus atom among a billion silicon atoms can raise conductivity thousands of times. An accidental impurity at twenty parts per billion can equal the lightest deliberate dose. Purity is therefore not polish. It is function.

The purified silicon melts at about 1,414 degrees. A seed crystal touches the melt and rises slowly, rotating as it pulls a single crystal behind it.

The melt rests in a high-purity quartz crucible. Spruce Pine returns here, not inside the chip, but around its birth.

A crucible survives only a few hundred hours of melt. Then the vessel is spent.

Workers slice the ingot with diamond wire. Each wafer is 775 micrometres thick. Polishing brings thickness variation down to about a micrometre. Surface roughness falls to fractions of a nanometre.

Only after that journey does sand become a wafer.

The mining map looks diversified. Congo produced an estimated 76% of mined cobalt in 2024, about 220,000 of 290,000 tonnes. Australia supplied about 32% of mined lithium in 2025. China supplied 21%, and Chile supplied 19%.

China mined about 69% of the world’s rare earth oxides. Copper came largely from Chile and Peru. At the mine gate, no single country owns the phone. That appearance ends at the refinery door.

A mine makes rock or concentrate. A phone needs metals and chemicals of extraordinary purity. Refining sits between those worlds. It is also where the map narrows to China.

The International Energy Agency’s 2025 outlook makes China the leading refiner for 19 of 20 important strategic minerals. Its average share is around 70%.

China handles roughly 90% of rare earth separation. It handles around 90% of graphite processing for battery anodes.

It refines about 70% of cobalt and about two-thirds of lithium chemicals. Copper is its weakest grip in this group, at 45%.

Australian lithium ore often travels to China for conversion. Congolese cobalt, much of it from Chinese-owned mines, follows the same route.

CMOC is the world’s largest single cobalt producer. Even so, production does not confer the same power as processing.

California rare earth ore has historically gone to China for separation. The separation plants, and the knowledge inside them, are there. Every material climbs a ladder. Copper ore starts at only 0.5 to 1% metal.

Flotation makes a concentrate of 20 to 35%. Smelting makes matte at about 60%. Another step produces blister copper at 98 to 99%. Electrorefining finishes the climb at 99.99% cathode.

Logic-board traces need that final rung. A one-percent rock cannot carry a signal through an iPhone. Lithium climbs more slowly. Atacama brine begins near 1,500 milligrams per litre and spends twelve to eighteen months in ponds.

It reaches about six percent lithium. Only 40 to 60% of the lithium survives the process. Hard-rock spodumene moves faster, but not gently. It is calcined above 1,000 degrees before its lithium can be leached.

Cobalt cannot answer a price signal. About 99% of it arrives as a byproduct of copper and nickel mining. No cobalt boom opens a cobalt mine by itself. The host metals set the pace.

Graphite is flaked and milled into spheres. It is purified beyond 99.95% carbon, then coated for the battery anode. China dominates that processing chain even more completely than it dominates graphite mining.

Rare earths demand the longest separation. Ore is first concentrated to about 60 or 70%. Acid or alkali cracks it open. Solvent extraction then moves the liquid through hundreds of counter-current stages.

The stages separate elements that behave almost identically. A magnet may need neodymium without much dysprosium, or a precise amount of each.

Aluminum uses force instead of subtlety. Bauxite becomes alumina, then the Hall-Heroult process turns it into metal.

Smelting takes thirteen to fifteen megawatt-hours per tonne. Electricity can reach 40% of the metal’s cost. Smelters therefore gather beside cheap power. Recycled aluminum uses about 95% less energy, which makes it valuable at Apple’s scale.

The honest summary is short. The dirt is global, and the chemistry is Chinese. Apple does not claim to know more than that for a particular phone. Its conflict-minerals filing maps suppliers to smelters and refiners.

Apple says it does not buy directly from mines. Origin information arrives in aggregate, and the origin of material in a specific part may remain unknown.

No one can truthfully name the mine behind the cobalt in one handset. Anyone who does is inventing the answer.

States have learned how quietly refining can be used. In February 2025, Congo banned cobalt exports outright.

By October, quotas replaced the ban. The limit is about 96,600 tonnes a year for 2026 and 2027, roughly half of 2024 exports.

Cobalt prices rose more than 160%. The restriction needed no factory, army, or embargo announcement. In April 2025, China placed seven rare earth elements under export licensing. Dysprosium and terbium were among them.

Those elements help an iPhone’s Taptic Engine move and its MagSafe magnets hold. A license can take weeks or months. The weapon is a queue. Mine owners learned that they could be price-takers even while owning the resource.

Apple’s counterweight is partly accounting. The iPhone 17 lists 100% recycled cobalt and 95% recycled lithium in its battery. Its boards use 100% recycled gold plating and tin solder. Its magnets use 100% recycled rare earths.

Read those claims precisely. Apple’s environmental reporting accounts for recycled cobalt by mass balance. Recycled and virgin material mix in the stream. The recycled share is then assigned on paper to products.

The procurement is real, and it limits Apple’s exposure to virgin supply. It does not mean the atoms in one phone came from another phone.

Daisy, Apple’s disassembly robot, can take apart up to 200 phones an hour. It works in Austin and Breda.

At theoretical full capacity, two Daisy sites could process roughly 1% of a year’s iPhone shipments. The loop is a hedge, not a circle. The phone still begins, overwhelmingly, in the dirt.

Chapter Two

The Furnace

In Taiwan, a company founded by a 55-year-old executive and a government that owned half of it prints the most complex objects humans mass-produce, and charges like it.

The most valuable step happens in a room kept almost impossibly clean. Its permitted particle counts run a hundred to ten thousand times below a hospital operating room’s.

The process takes about three months. A blank wafer enters, and a finished processor leaves.

The wafer tells the earlier story again. Quartz becomes silicon, silicon becomes a crystal, and the crystal is sliced and polished nearly flat at atomic scale.

Five firms supply more than 90% of the world’s 300mm wafers. Two of them are Japanese.

On that disc, TSMC builds the processor Apple designed. It prints one layer, changes it, and prints the next.

The fab follows a grammar. Every layer begins with a clean wafer. A film is deposited from gas or vapour. It may be only a few atoms thick, or a few hundred nanometres.

Photoresist coats the film. Light prints the layer’s pattern into that coating. Plasma or wet chemistry etches what the pattern exposes. Dopant ions then enter the open silicon. Boron serves one polarity. Phosphorus or arsenic serves the other.

Heat anneals the damaged crystal and activates the dopants. A slurry and pad polish the surface flat again. Flatness matters because the next exposure needs a plane on which to focus. Then the loop starts over.

The lower layers become transistors. The upper ten to fifteen layers become copper wiring. Each copper layer is made by etching trenches, lining them, filling them with electroplated copper, and polishing away the excess.

The method is called damascene. It borrows its name from metalworkers who inlaid one metal into another in Damascus. A processor needs roughly eighty to a hundred and twenty layers. It needs about ninety mask exposures.

The whole route contains five hundred to a thousand discrete steps. A wafer leaves fourteen to sixteen weeks after it entered.

Much of that time is waiting. The wafer waits for the next machine, the next inspection, and the next clean.

The light creates the narrowest gate. Ordinary deep ultraviolet light has a wavelength of 193 nanometres. At the smallest features, that light needs repeated exposures. Cost and error multiply with each pass.

Extreme ultraviolet light works at 13.5 nanometres. It solves one problem and creates several others. Air absorbs EUV.

Glass absorbs it too. The scanner therefore runs in a vacuum and focuses with mirrors. Its light begins as molten tin.

ASML fires droplets about twenty-five micrometres wide through the chamber. It fires fifty thousand of them each second. A first laser pulse flattens each droplet. A second vaporises it into plasma, which flashes at 13.5 nanometres.

One scanner costs about $180 to $200 million. It weighs about 180 tonnes and contains more than a hundred thousand parts. The high-numerical-aperture successor costs around $380 million. ASML is the only company that sells such a machine.

The first 3-nanometre generation used EUV for as many as twenty-five layers. The refined generation reduced that number to nineteen. Every EUV pass costs money and time. Fewer passes mean a process has learned how to breathe.

A fab full of these tools costs an estimated $15 to $20 billion. Most of the money buys equipment, not the building.

Published project splits put tools at about half to four-fifths of the total. The range matters because no two fabs divide the bill alike.

Five suppliers divide the work. ASML owns lithography. Applied Materials sells the broadest range: deposition, etch, implantation, and polishing.

Lam Research concentrates on etch and deposition. Tokyo Electron coats and cleans. KLA inspects and measures, hunting the defects the other machines create.

The building also consumes at industrial scale. TSMC used 161 litres of water per wafer mask layer in 2024. The figure fell to 153 litres in 2025. TSMC recycled 88% of its process water in 2024.

A large fab draws power continuously, on the scale of a small city. The furnace never really cools.

TSMC began with a refusal. Morris Chang had spent 25 years at Texas Instruments and rose to lead its semiconductor business.

Inside TI in 1976, Chang proposed a factory that made only other companies’ chips. TI rejected the idea.

Taiwan recruited him in 1985 to lead the Industrial Technology Research Institute. TSMC was incorporated in Hsinchu on February 21, 1987.

The government development fund held 48.3%. Philips held 27.5%, and the company began with about $220 million in capital. The invention was a promise. TSMC would never sell chips that competed with its customers.

That promise made the fabless industry possible. A designer could hand TSMC its plans without arming a rival. Apple bought PA Semi for $278 million in 2008. Its first processor, the A4, shipped in 2010.

Samsung made the A4. Apple later moved flagship production to TSMC. TSMC has made Apple’s leading-edge phone processors alone since the A10 in 2016. The relationship now looks less like sourcing than dependence.

The furnace charges accordingly. A current-generation wafer costs an estimated $18,000 to $20,000. That is roughly twice the 7-nanometre wafer price in 2018.

Counterpoint estimated that the A17 Pro added about $30 to each phone, mostly from the process.

TSMC spent about $41 billion on capital equipment in 2025. Apple spent $12.7 billion. TSMC’s gross margin was 59.9% on $122.9 billion of revenue. Apple supplies roughly a quarter of that revenue.

The dependence runs both ways, but not evenly. Apple can survive a late delivery more easily than it can replace the supplier.

No other company can make a 3-nanometre-class chip for a quarter-billion phones. There is no second source waiting.

Taiwan’s rules keep the newest processes on the island. TSMC’s Arizona plants, backed by a $165 billion US commitment, run generations behind. Arizona produces wafers, not finished phones. Geography changes slowly at the front of the chain.

A finished wafer is not yet a chip. Probe needles touch every die and test it first. Packaging a dead die would waste money. Failures are mapped and discarded before the wafer moves on.

An A17 Pro die covers about 104 square millimetres. A 300mm wafer holds roughly 616 dies by geometry. Analysts independently estimated about 620. At the first generation’s reported yield of about 55%, only some 340 worked.

The wafer is ground thin and diced with a diamond blade. Good dies then enter packaging, also at TSMC in Taiwan. The die sits in a reconstituted wafer of epoxy. Its connections fan outward through redistribution layers.

Memory is stacked directly on top. TSMC has used this package-on-package arrangement for Apple’s chips since the A10 in 2016.

The design needs no substrate and saves thickness. The pair is tested again at temperature extremes and sorted into bins.

Only then is the brain a component. It was designed by Apple, fabricated by TSMC, and married to memory without leaving Taiwan.

The first footnote concerns the name. “3 nanometres” names a generation, not a feature. No part of the chip measures 3 nanometres across. The tightest pitches run around 24 to 45 nanometres.

Memory cells have barely shrunk across two generations. Each new node therefore costs more and delivers less than the last.

The second footnote concerns who paid for Apple’s priority. At the first 3-nanometre launch, reported yields were around 55%.

Apple reportedly paid for each working die, not each wafer. TSMC absorbed the dead dies during the first generation. That bargain funded the yield ramp. Later customers inherited a process Apple had helped pay to stabilise.

The bargain is changing. AI accelerators now take most of TSMC’s leading-edge growth. Apple remains a huge customer. It is no longer the only bidder that matters at the frontier.

The furnace still runs for Apple. It no longer runs only for Apple.

Chapter Three

The Parts

Between the furnace and the assembly line sits a layer of firms that make exactly one thing better than anyone alive, and charge rent for it in different currencies.

Take an iPhone apart and the pile becomes a map. Each part marks a firm that learned to do one thing exceptionally well.

Almost nothing is a simple commodity. Almost nothing is made by the company whose name appears on the box.

The screen is Korean. Samsung Display and LG Display supplied about 99% of iPhone 17 panels through October 2025.

China’s BOE supplies older and entry models. In 2026 reporting, it was shut out of the premium line after failing the flagship specification.

Apple needs LG for a reason beyond supply. LG gives Samsung a credible rival. Analysts estimate that Apple provides roughly a third of LG Display’s revenue. That dependence limits LG’s leverage, while its existence limits Samsung’s.

Samsung can make the foldable panel and the newest phone OLED generation. That capability gives it the stronger hand.

Apple has bought leverage before. In 2017, it was reported to have put about $2.67 billion into LG’s OLED factories.

The money tried to build a second source into existence. Apple often purchases competition the way other firms purchase parts. The panel explains the difficulty. A flexible OLED starts as polyimide plastic deposited on glass.

The glass is only a carrier. The plastic rides it through the factory and separates from it at the end. Workers build a transistor backplane on the plastic. The steps resemble chipmaking: deposit, print, etch, and repeat.

The silicon begins amorphous. Excimer laser annealing crystallises it into LTPS. Premium LTPO panels add oxide transistors. They leak less current in the switching role.

That lower leakage lets the display vary its refresh rate from one hertz to a hundred and twenty. A still picture can sip power.

The light-emitting layer arrives by evaporation. In a vacuum chamber, organics pass through a fine metal mask onto the panel. The mask has an opening for every subpixel. Three passes lay down red, green, and blue.

Canon Tokki supplies most of the evaporation machines. Another narrow gate hides inside the screen factory. Thin-film encapsulation seals the organics immediately. Unprotected, they can degrade within hours in air.

A laser finally lifts the finished panel from its glass carrier. Every step creates a chance to lose the panel.

BOE passed Apple’s approval and then failed in production. The episode shows what a decade of yield learning is worth.

The camera eye is Japanese. Sony began researching image sensors in 1970. Sony shipped back-illuminated CMOS products in 2009.

It introduced the first stacked sensor in 2012. Its sensors entered the iPhone with the 4S in 2011. Sony has supplied every iPhone generation since.

The sensors are made in Kumamoto. Sony holds roughly half the world market for phone camera sensors.

A sensor is not a part Apple can swap casually. It is developed with the image processor in Apple’s chip across generations.

That joint learning creates the chokepoint. The supplier knows the customer’s future because it helped design it. Apple’s August 2025 announcement contained one vague and important sentence. It mentioned new chip technology with Samsung in Austin, Texas.

Later reporting identified the chips as image sensors. They would serve products including the iPhone. If the reporting is right, Sony’s fourteen-year exclusivity will end from a Texas fab. Apple has not confirmed the identification.

The pattern matters more than the announcement. When a supplier becomes irreplaceable, Apple spends years building a replacement. Sony’s sensor is two chips acting as one. The lower wafer handles logic, readout, and processing.

The upper wafer carries the pixel array. Its process is tuned for light rather than computation. Sony thins and flips that wafer. Light reaches the photodiodes from the back, without first crossing the wiring.

Modern versions bond the wafers face to face. Copper pads fuse directly to copper pads. A colour filter mosaic sits above the stack. A microlens is printed over every pixel.

The lens above it contains seven plastic elements in a typical flagship main camera. Each element corrects errors introduced by the others. Taiwan’s Largan Precision makes most of those lenses. The plastic is not the hard part.

The mould is. Its contours are held to a few tenths of a micrometre, cavity after cavity. A voice-coil motor moves the lens stack to focus. Coils and magnets work against springs.

The stabiliser shifts the lens, or the whole sensor, against the gyroscope’s reading of a hand’s movement. None of this comes from a catalogue at Apple’s standard. The cover glass is American. Its favourite origin story is false.

Corning did not revive a shelved 1960s windshield product. Its own FAQ calls that account a myth. Corning carried expertise from the 1960s, not a finished glass waiting for a phone. The distinction matters.

Six months before the first iPhone shipped in 2007, Steve Jobs scratched a plastic prototype with his keys. He demanded glass.

Corning developed a new composition in under six months. Every iPhone generation since has used glass made in Harrodsburg, Kentucky.

Apple’s Advanced Manufacturing Fund supplied $495 million between 2017 and 2021. That money helped produce Ceramic Shield.

In August 2025, Apple committed another $2.5 billion to Harrodsburg. The plant is to make all cover glass for iPhone and Watch.

That is a commitment, not yet a shipment record. Corning gained a plant devoted to one customer. Apple gained a major component that tariffs cannot easily reach. The exchange explains both companies’ loyalty.

Fusion draw gives the glass its surface. Molten glass feeds into a V-shaped trough called an isopipe. It overflows both edges evenly. The two streams run down the faces and meet at the root.

They fuse in air into one sheet. Neither outer surface has touched a roller, a tin bath, or a tool. The surfaces emerge pristine. They need no grinding or polishing to become usable.

Chemistry adds strength later. The cut sheet enters molten potassium salt at about 400 degrees. Smaller sodium ions leave the glass. Larger potassium ions take their places in spaces slightly too small for them.

The crowding creates compression at the surface. A crack must fight that squeeze before it can open. Ceramic Shield adds Apple’s own deposited technology. The foundation remains Corning’s untouched sheet and its compressed skin.

The frame has its own industrial history. Apple’s aluminium unibody began with the 2008 MacBook. Machines borrowed from aerospace practice milled it from a single block. Current Pro phones start closer to their final form.

The aluminium is heat-forged first. CNC machines finish it to tolerance. Anodising then turns the frame into the anode in a sulphuric acid bath. Its surface becomes aluminium oxide, five to twenty-five micrometres thick.

The layer is not paint. It is a conversion of the metal itself. Its pores take dye, then near-boiling water seals them shut. Colour becomes part of the skin.

Titanium shows the cost of another choice. It conducts heat poorly, so cutting heat stays at the tool tip.

It galls, welds to cutters, and hardens as it is cut. Production runs slowly and consumes tooling. Apple diffusion-bonded titanium to an internal aluminium structure. Titanium faces the hand and eye.

Aluminium handles the heat inside. The bond joins the two metals atom to atom. Memory belongs to three firms. Samsung, SK hynix, and Micron make more than 95% of the world’s DRAM.

They have found a more urgent customer. AI servers use about three times the wafer capacity per unit of memory as phone memory does.

Capacity has moved toward data centres. A 12GB phone module rose from about $30 in early 2025 to about $70 by late 2025.

Apple buyers were reported staying in hotels near Korean memory plants. The company that once summoned suppliers was queuing. The radios rest on a treaty. Qualcomm’s patent license was renewed in September 2026, effective in April 2027.

The charge is based on the price of the whole phone. It survives even when Apple’s own modem supplies the silicon.

The license covers the cellular standard itself. Apple cannot design around the standard and keep a working phone.

Apple bought most of Intel’s modem business for about $1 billion in 2019. Its first modem, the C1, reached the iPhone 16e in February 2025. Apple still pays Qualcomm. Escape remains incomplete.

Broadcom’s filters present the same problem in physical form. In July 2026, Apple committed more than $30 billion through 2031. The agreement covers over 15 billion US-made chips. Broadcom’s filters are made in Fort Collins, Colorado.

Underneath them sits Murata. About 1,300 Murata ceramic capacitors regulate power across an iPhone 17 board. Murata holds about 40% of that market and makes its own ceramic powder. It cannot be replaced from spot supply.

A bad lot of a part costing a fraction of a cent can stop the line. Cheap does not mean unimportant.

A Broadcom filter works because sound is slow. Its core is a film of piezoelectric aluminium nitride between electrodes.

The film hangs over a cavity. A radio signal makes the film itself ring. The standing acoustic wave resonates when the film is half a wavelength thick. Sound moves tens of thousands of times more slowly than light.

A gigahertz resonator can therefore fit inside a film a few micrometres thick. An electromagnetic version of similar quality would be far larger and lossier.

The advantage is a constant of nature, manufactured well. That is why the filter is a treaty, not a purchase order.

The magnets begin as powder. Neodymium, iron, and boron are melted and strip-cast onto a spinning, water-cooled copper wheel. The alloy freezes into flakes a fraction of a millimetre thick. Speed keeps its structure fine.

Hydrogen enters the grain boundaries and expands the lattice. The material breaks itself apart from inside. Nitrogen jet mills reduce the powder to three to five micrometres. A magnetic field aligns the grains during pressing.

Vacuum sintering above 1,000 degrees makes a dense magnet. Workers then machine it, coat it against corrosion, and magnetise it. Those magnets hold MagSafe in place. They also drive the speaker and steady the camera.

The Taptic Engine uses a linear version. A mass rides on springs while a coil and magnet drive it along one axis.

It starts and stops at resonance so quickly that the phone taps instead of buzzes. The sensation is mechanics timed precisely.

The battery returns the story to refining. ATL makes most of its cells in China. Its graphite anode is processed overwhelmingly in China. Its cathode chemicals are also refined mostly there.

The phone’s most advanced chemistry sits deepest inside the refining map. Assembly is not the concentration that matters most. Making a cell is mostly controlled time. Cathode powder becomes a slurry with conductive carbon and binder.

A slot die coats that slurry onto aluminium foil. Graphite is coated onto copper foil for the anode. Heated polished rollers dry and compress the coated foils. Machines slit them to width.

Layers are stacked in a dry room: cathode, separator, anode. Tabs are welded, the stack is pouched, and electrolyte enters under vacuum. Formation comes next. During the first slow charge, electrolyte decomposes against the graphite surface on purpose.

The residue becomes the solid electrolyte interphase. It blocks electrons, passes ions, and shapes the cell’s safety and life. Formation takes a day or two. Formation and aging together can take up to three weeks.

Cells rest at controlled temperatures while workers watch voltage. A tell-tale sag reveals a defect.

Review literature puts formation alone at up to a third of cell production cost. Formation and aging also take the largest share of floor space.

The hidden input is time. A cell maker pays for three weeks of expensive floor before the cell can power anything.

Finished cells are graded by capacity and resistance. Sunwoda and Desay then add protection circuitry and flex cables.

The cells remain ATL’s. The battery is a chemical product, a real estate problem, and a Chinese refining story in one part.

Chapter Four

The Hands

The famous step is the cheapest one. Its real product is not phones but surge capacity: a quarter of a million people, assembled as fast as the phones are.

Assembly begins as something else. It begins as organisation. Apple once made its own computers. Tim Cook joined from Compaq in March 1998 and started dismantling that system.

Within his first years, key suppliers fell from about a hundred to twenty-four. Components made in-house were sold to their suppliers or moved out.

Apple began buying factory capacity instead of owning factories. It contracted the production and kept the design. Inventory told the story. Cook cut it from about a month of stock to six days by September 1998.

Unsold inventory fell from about $400 million to $78 million. The machine worked on information instead of stock.

Apple closed its last major US assembly plant in Elk Grove, California, in April 2004. The centre of production moved east.

Foxconn had already been waiting there. Terry Gou founded Hon Hai in 1974.

Foxconn opened its first mainland plant at Longhua, Shenzhen, in 1988. The campus became a city of its own.

Its dormitories, canteens, and clinics made the workforce itself an internal market. Revenue rose from $1.8 billion in 1999 to $98 billion in 2010.

At launch, the iPhone almost failed on its surface. Jobs showed a plastic prototype screen scratched by his keys. He ordered glass instead, about six months before shipment. Supplier Corning developed the glass, but integration became manufacturing’s emergency.

A former Apple executive told the New York Times what happened in Shenzhen. At midnight, about 8,000 workers were roused from dormitories.

Each received a biscuit and a cup of tea. A shift had begun installing glass screens.

Within 96 hours, the plant made more than ten thousand glass-screen iPhones a day. The story is the assembly model in perfect form.

It is also the whole truth in one direction. A housed, mobilised workforce could perform at a speed no ordinary labour market could match.

By 2016, the factory city had moved to Zhengzhou. The New York Times called Zhengzhou iPhone City. The Times counted more than $1.5 billion in government support. Support arrived as land, power, infrastructure, bonuses, and tax support.

Henan made an early $250 million loan. It gave $56 million in subsidies during the plant’s first two years. The operation received discounted energy and transport. The government built a special customs zone and recruited labour.

Peak employment reached about 350,000 in the Times’ account. At full pace, the plant made 500,000 phones a day. Zhengzhou was not merely cheap labour. It was a state industrial platform built around one product.

China Labor Watch returned in September 2025. Its account is a range, not Apple’s September figure. The group estimated 150,000 to 200,000 workers at peak. It estimated 60,000 to 80,000 regular workers.

Dispatch workers supplied another 80,000 to 110,000 people. The range matters because the workforce itself rises and falls with the phone.

Regular base pay was RMB 2,100 to 2,400, roughly $295 to $335. China Labor Watch said base pay had been flat since 2019.

Overtime and bonuses brought a typical month to about RMB 3,000. Dispatch recruitment set a record bonus of RMB 9,800.

Part of the dispatch premium is deferred. A worker who resigns before a set date can wait 45 to 50 days for the second installment.

The recruitment structure built the ramp and held it. Flexibility for Apple meant waiting built into workers’ pay. Recruitment fees were the abuse Apple did find. Apple has repaid $34.5 million to more than 37,700 workers since 2008.

Workers had paid the fees before Apple prohibited them. Later audits found the practice had continued.

India begins from a different wage. Reuters documented about $140 a month in 2021, at about ₹10,500.

Workers were commonly hired through contractors. They paid the contractor for hostel housing and food. Ages were mostly eighteen to twenty-two.

The system’s fragility appeared in December 2021. Food poisoning closed a marquee Indian plant after workers protested. Reuters had documented a marriage-exclusion policy at Sriperumbudur. It barred women who married from these jobs.

The policy was rationalised as preventing attrition. Foxconn corrected it only after Reuters published the account. Those are the hands at market rate. Inside the campus, the work runs in two halves.

Only one half is the photograph. The first half is the board, and it is machines.

About 2,700 distinct parts go into a phone, drawn from more than two hundred suppliers. The logic board takes the densest share of them.

A stencil prints solder paste onto the bare board. The paste is flux and microscopic spheres of SAC305 alloy, 96.5% tin.

A 3D inspection machine measures every paste deposit before anything is placed. An error caught here costs nothing; the same error caught later costs the board.

Pick-and-place machines then set the components. The smallest measure four tenths of a millimetre by two tenths.

Each part is optically centred and placed at tens of thousands per hour. The board rides through a reflow oven peaking near 245 degrees, which melts the paste into joints.

Cameras inspect the result. X-ray machines inspect what cameras cannot see: the joints hidden under the processor and the radio chips.

Only then does the board meet a human being. The final station shows why it still needs one.

Final assembly, test, and packaging takes roughly four hundred steps. The New York Times counted them in 2016. Workers screw the board into the frame. They place the battery on stretch-release adhesive.

Cameras, the Taptic Engine, and speakers follow. A perimeter gasket carries the water-resistance rating before the back closes. The sequence is human because the parts are floppy and fragile. Each one is slightly different.

A line must also double within eight weeks. Steel automation cannot be rebuilt every September at that speed. The line then becomes a measuring machine. Each camera module is aligned while it watches a test pattern.

Lens and sensor move sideways, in and out, and by tip, tilt, and rotation. The module is fixed where that individual unit is sharpest.

Each display is corrected for mura. The panel is measured, and a correction is stored for its driver chip.

The correction is applied pixel by pixel. The finished phone is pressurised and listened to for leaks. Water resistance is tested with air, never water. On filmed lines, a failed phone is not patched.

It is completely disassembled. Its parts are retested, and it returns to the start of the line. An iPhone 6s teardown counted fifty-eight screws. Each measured under a millimetre, and together they weighed about a gram.

A modern line turns that patience into an industry. The patience is exactly what Apple buys. India now assembles roughly one iPhone in four. About 55 million were assembled there in 2025.

That is about 25% of global output of 220 to 230 million phones. The year before, India assembled about 36 million.

Every iPhone 17 model, including the Pros, was assembled in India from launch. The driver was not wages.

China answered the transfer directly. In mid-2025, Chinese engineers and technicians were recalled from iPhone lines in India. Beijing had pressed Foxconn over the transfer. Reports put the recalled count between about 300 and about 600.

The people who know how to run the lines became a controlled export. Knowledge moved slower than factories. The assemblers reshuffled at the same time. Pegatron, once Apple’s second maker, ceded its flagship Kunshan campus to Luxshare.

Pegatron also handed operating control of its only Indian iPhone plant to Tata. It kept a 40% minority stake.

Tata bought Wistron’s Indian iPhone business for $125 million in November 2023. It took 60% of Pegatron’s Indian unit in January 2025.

Tata now controls three of the four iPhone assemblers in India. A new national champion is forming at the least valuable step. Luxshare began by making cables. It now takes about 71% of its revenue from Apple.

Luxshare earns component margins on top of assembly margins. It climbed the chain while others defended the bottom. Why assemble in India at this scale? Not because the work is simply cheaper there.

India pays companies to come. Its production-linked incentive returns 4 to 6% of incremental sales in cash. That payment is larger than the assembler’s entire net profit margin on the work. The subsidy exceeds the profit.

India is buying the learning curve. China made the same purchase at Zhengzhou with land and loans. The United States is attempting its own version. Apple’s $600 billion commitment funds components, glass, lasers, and servers.

It pointedly does not fund iPhone assembly. Even Washington prices the steps differently. Assembly moves to whoever pays for the privilege of hosting it. The step is worth so little that governments can outbid the wage bill.

The sequel is already visible. India assembled the phones in 2025 from parts that still arrive from the old map. Processors, displays, memory, and cameras came from Taiwan, Korea, and Japan. The flag on the box changed.

The chain inside it mostly did not.

Chapter Five

The Flight

A finished iPhone is worth so much per kilogram that the sky is its natural habitat, and time, not freight, is the cost being bought.

A finished phone weighs about 350 grams in its box, against a $1,199 retail price.

That value density explains the airport. Two to four dollars of air freight add little to a $1,199 phone.

A 747 freighter can hold on the order of 150,000 phones. Zhengzhou’s airport made iPhone logistics a municipal strategy.

The pack-out is part of the speed. Phones are boxed, wrapped, and palletised inside the plant.

The customs post sits in the bonded zone a few hundred yards past the gate. A phone can be an export before it has left the campus fence.

Local records reported as many as 90 freighter flights in a single peak-season day. The bonded zone around the airport works around the clock.

The box itself was redesigned for the sky. Since the iPhone 12 in October 2020, it has carried no charger and no earbuds.

Apple announced the change as environmental, and it was that too. Two billion of its adapters and seven hundred million wired headphones were already in circulation.

Removal also shrank the box. Apple counts seventy percent more boxes to a pallet.

Since 2024 the box has been entirely fibre-based. What ships in it now is the phone, a one-metre USB-C cable, and paper.

Every gram removed is multiplied by two hundred million phones a year. The most consequential packaging decision Apple ever made was a removal.

The carriers’ leverage is capacity at two moments: the September launch, and the day a tariff changes. March 2025 was the purest demonstration on record.

Apple’s March 2025 airlift was insurance, not a stunt. A reciprocal tariff on India loomed for early April. Foxconn shipped $1.31 billion of iPhones from India that month, as much as its January and February combined. Tata shipped another $612 million.

The combined total was an all-time monthly record, nearly $2 billion. About 600 tons were airlifted, perhaps 1.5 million phones.

Chennai customs clearance was lobbied down from thirty hours to six. The rushed date mattered more than the route.

India’s assembled output escaped the China rate. Washington had warned that the lower Indian rate would end. Every week mattered.

Phones landed before the tariff could catch them. The gamble worked because smartphones were removed from the reciprocal scheme in April. The phones kept their exclusion.

A separate 20% duty still applied to Chinese-made smartphones from February. Policy had selected the assembly country. Apple counted the cost in results. Tariff costs were about $800 million in the June 2025 quarter.

Apple expected about $1.1 billion in the next quarter at rates then in force. Those were Cook’s figures on the July 2025 earnings call.

The flight ends at a carrier store because Americans buy phones through carriers. The carrier controls the first sale.

Apple took about 40% of its fiscal 2025 net sales directly, and 60% through others. In the United States, CIRP credits carriers with about three quarters of iPhone sales.

Apple sells about one in seven phones itself. Its screens receive the pricing and financing offers carriers place on them.

After the sale, the phone leaves Apple’s chain and enters another. The trade-in terms run on Apple’s clock. A traded device must reach Apple’s vendor within fourteen days. Ownership passes to that vendor, whose pipeline runs wipe, inspect, grade, repair, and resale.

Counterpoint found refurbished iPhone sales in India grew 19% in the first half of 2025. Africa was the fastest-growing used-phone region at 6%. Workhorse models there were the iPhone 11 and 12.

Two flows matter here. Regions differ by income, while one model serves the bottom of both markets. The older phone keeps working after the first chain closes. It becomes the entry product in another market.

That geography shadows the first one. Apple’s chain extends beyond the first buyer and beyond the first country.

Chapter Six

The Price

What the buyer at the counter is actually purchasing is not the pile of parts. The pile is the smaller half of the money.

There are two kinds of price in the story. One is the bill of materials; the other is the margin chain.

TD Cowen priced a 256GB iPhone 16 Pro Max at $485 in components, box, and assembly.

The retail price was $1,199. The BOM captures about 40% of it. The display cost about $80. The rear camera cost about $80.

The processor, memory, radios, and hundreds of smaller parts make up the rest. BOM excludes research, software, logistics, marketing, warranty, returns, and retail rent.

It also excludes the value of services sold after the phone. The $485 is a floor, not the phone’s full cost.

The previous model shows the range between teardown firms. Counterpoint put its BOM at $502, while Nikkei and Fomalhaut put it at $558. The difference was $56. The two estimates are boundaries, not photocopies of an Apple ledger.

Vendor choice changes a BOM. Memory-cycle timing changes it too. Storage capacity changes it again. Anyone who gives the figure to a cent is inventing precision.

Apple does not report an iPhone gross margin. The nearest public figure is Products gross margin for FY2025: 36.8%.

That category includes iPhone, Mac, iPad, Watch, and AirPods. Treat it as an upper guide, not an iPhone figure. The chain explains the split.

TSMC kept 59.9 cents of every revenue dollar as gross profit. Apple’s Products margin was 36.8%. Hon Hai’s gross margin was 6.25%, and its net margin was 2.23%.

Assembly is contestable. Fabrication is scarce, and scarcity keeps the difference.

The scale cannot be mistaken for lack of success. Apple’s iPhone net sales were $209.6 billion in FY2025. They were $201.2 billion in FY2024 and $200.6 billion in FY2023. Total company net sales were $416.2 billion.

Anyone expecting a margin to fall should watch those sales first. They are not falling. One payment term finances the machine. Apple pays suppliers in about 115 days on average.

It collects from many customers sooner. Suppliers effectively fund the interval. Negative working capital was designed into Cook’s system. It is part of why scale compounds.

The phone also buys an annuity. Services carry a gross margin of 75.4%, against 36.8% for hardware.

The comparison explains why holding the customer matters more than squeezing parts. Hardware pays once, services keep paying. Apple’s 115-day supplier terms build the annuity’s working capital. One customer becomes a stream rather than a transaction.

Suppliers carry the production interval. Apple carries the relationship. The phone then keeps paying after its first sale.

It can outlive two owners and still produce service revenue. Research funding completes the account. Apple spent $34.6 billion on R&D in FY2025.

SG&A cost $27.6 billion. Together they were about $62 billion, around 15% of sales. Research does not arrive by manufacture. It is bought with the margin left after the chain is paid.

Chapter Seven

Houston and Texas

Texas is in your iPhone. Just not in the way the speeches say, and Houston, the energy capital, is barely in it at all.

No iPhone is assembled in Texas. The simplified version is correct. Texas makes components for other Apple products.

It makes one iPhone component of consequence. Coherent’s lasers live behind the user’s face. They scan it in infrared to unlock the phone.

VCSELs for Face ID are made in Sherman, Texas. Apple and Coherent announced a multiyear agreement on August 7, 2025.

The laser uses a vertical cavity and a surface emitter. It can be fabricated and tested like a semiconductor.

That production fits a wafer fab. It does not fit the assembly-line image attached to reshoring. GlobalWafers America opened in Sherman on May 15, 2025. The project cost $3.5 billion.

It was the first advanced 300mm wafer facility built in the United States in more than twenty years.

Its silicon can enter TSMC Arizona and TI’s Sherman fab. In August 2025, Apple partnered with GlobalWafers. Texas silicon can now feed Apple processors and Texas Instruments chips.

Apple signed a $500 million agreement with MP Materials on July 15, 2025. MP will make neodymium magnets in Fort Worth. Lines at the Independence facility are set to ship magnets from 2027.

Texas has one real Houston story. Apple’s 250,000-square-foot server factory builds Private Cloud Compute servers.

Those servers shipped in October 2025. They run Apple Intelligence queries too sensitive for the phone.

In February 2026, Apple said Mac mini production would join the site later that year. The campus would double to about 500,000 square feet.

The Houston plant does not make phones. It makes the computers that answer them. Another Texas supply line belongs to Tesla. Its Robstown refinery began feeding a rotary kiln in December 2024.

Tesla announced it fully operational in January 2026. It is North America’s first plant turning spodumene into lithium hydroxide. Robstown feeds Tesla’s own batteries. It proves the chemistry can be rebuilt in Texas, even outside Apple’s chain.

Texas remembers a larger role. Samsung’s Austin fab made the A5 for the iPhone 4S. Full production began in December 2011.

The brain of an iPhone was once Texan. TSMC took that work. Apple has been in Austin since 1992 and employs more than thirteen thousand Texans.

Design, services, and Daisy live there. Manufacture mostly does not.

The Mac Pro explains the distance. One production detail became a parable of screws. A twenty-employee Texas machine shop could make at most a thousand custom screws a day. The screws were ordered from China instead.

A factory is an ecosystem, not a building with workers inside. Apple discontinued the Mac Pro in March 2026. The server plant is the newest chapter, not a reversal. Texas contributes silicon, lasers, magnets, servers, and recycling.

It does not assemble the phone. The state’s role is growing at the points where scarcity pays.

Chapter Eight

Two Rival Reads

Two coherent ways to read the same chain. Each names the evidence that would settle it.

Read One

The chain is a stack of chokepoints, and the stack is stable.

On this read, nothing important has moved in a decade. Every attempt to move a chokepoint has failed, cost a fortune, or produced a token plant.

Processors are still made in Taiwan. Displays still come from Korea, and sensors still come from Japan.

Assembly’s move to India changes the flag, not the structure. The components inside Indian phones still come from the old map.

Decide by: India’s local component value stays small through 2028 even as assembly share rises; TSMC’s newest nodes stay Taiwan-only; and the next tariff shock moves assembly again without touching the component map.

Read Two

The chokepoints themselves are starting to move, because the buyer above Apple changed.

On this read, the important event of 2025 and 2026 is not India. It is AI demand.

AI has made Apple a price-taker at two layers it used to command. Those layers are TSMC’s frontier capacity and the memory oligopoly’s wafers.

A chain loses its shape when its anchor tenant loses allocation. It gets rebuilt around the new anchor.

Apple’s response is the early shape of a second component map. It includes sensors in Texas, glass in Kentucky, a $30 billion filter agreement, and magnet lines in Fort Worth.

The new map is American-anchored. It is subsidised the way Zhengzhou was.

Decide by: Samsung’s Austin sensors actually shipping in an iPhone generation; Apple publicly taking a minority share of a frontier node’s first allocation and saying so; memory contracts repricing Apple’s hardware margin down in filed results, extending the FY2025 dip to 36.8% beyond the tariff costs already attributed to it.

The decider is measurable. Watch where the components in an India-assembled iPhone are made in 2028.

Watch, too, whether Apple’s name is still first on TSMC’s newest node.

Chapter Nine

Watchlist

Five developments, each tied to a claim in this report. Each one moves a specific part of the analysis when it lands.

  • 1Samsung’s Austin image sensors. Apple’s August 2025 language was deliberately vague; reporting says camera sensors for a 2027 iPhone. If they ship, Sony’s fourteen-year sole-source ends, and Texas gains its first component actually inside the current phone at scale beyond Face ID lasers.
  • 2TSMC’s frontier capacity. AI accelerators are taking the majority of TSMC’s leading-edge growth, and Apple now shares the front of a queue it once effectively owned. TSMC’s smartphone-versus-HPC revenue split through 2027 is the measure.
  • 3The memory contracts. DRAM prices are set in long-term agreements now being renegotiated. If the reported doubling of module prices reaches Apple’s filed hardware margin, the AI build-out will have taxed the iPhone directly.
  • 4India’s component test. Assembly is there; the question is whether displays, camera modules, and other components follow by 2028. Local component value, not assembly share, decides whether India is a new map or a new flag.
  • 5The refining weapon. Congo’s cobalt quotas run through 2027, and China’s rare-earth licensing is in force. Any extension, tightening, or first use against a named Western buyer turns a background condition into the story.
